content: The Guidelines on Verification of Measles Elimination in the Western Pacific Region were developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2013 to provide a framework for assessing and confirming the elimination of measles in countries and areas within the region. These guidelines outline the principles, processes, and criteria necessary for verification, as well as the roles of national and regional verification committees. Key Definitions and Concepts: 1. Measles Elimination: This refers to the interruption of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 12 months in the presence of a well-functioning surveillance system. 2. Endemic Measles Transmission: Continuous transmission of indigenous or imported measles virus persisting for 12 months or more in a defined geographical area. 3. Measles Outbreak in an Elimination Setting: A single laboratory-confirmed case of measles. 4. Laboratory-Confirmed Measles Case: A suspected case confirmed by a proficient laboratory. 5. Imported Case: A case exposed to measles outside the region or country during the 7–21 days before rash onset. 6. Import-Related Case: A locally acquired infection linked to an imported case through epidemiological or virological evidence. Progress in the Western Pacific Region: Since the goal of measles elimination was established in 2003, the region has made significant progress. Between 2008 and 2012, measles cases decreased by 93%, reaching a historic low of 9 cases per million population in 2012. By the end of 2012, endemic measles virus transmission may have been interrupted in as many as 33 countries and areas, including the 21 Pacific island countries and areas considered as one epidemiological block. However, endemic transmission still persisted in a few countries as of March 2013. Verification Process: The verification of measles elimination involves three essential criteria: 1. Interruption of Endemic Transmission: Documentation of the absence of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 months since the last known endemic case. 2. Surveillance Standards: The presence of a verification-standard surveillance system capable of detecting and classifying suspected measles cases. 3. Genotyping Evidence: Laboratory evidence supporting the interruption of endemic measles virus transmission. Lines of Evidence: Verification is based on five lines of evidence: 1. Epidemiology: A detailed analysis of measles incidence and epidemiology since the introduction of the measles vaccine, including classification of cases by source of infection and method of confirmation. 2. Surveillance Quality: 3. Population Immunity: Analysis of immunity levels, including marginalized and migrant groups, to demonstrate sufficient protection against measles. 4. Sustainability of Immunization Programs: Evidence of robust national immunization programs, including resources for mass campaigns to sustain elimination. 5. Genotyping Evidence: Molecular evidence confirming the absence of endemic measles virus strains. Surveillance and Laboratory Systems: All countries in the region conduct case-based, laboratory-supported surveillance for measles. Between 2007 and 2012, the completeness of monthly reporting to the WHO Regional Office increased from 51% to 99%, and timeliness improved from 19% to 92%. Adequate blood specimens were collected from 91% of suspected cases, exceeding the target of 80%. The regional measles and rubella laboratory network includes 383 laboratories, which tested specimens from over 18,500 suspected cases in 2012. Verification Committees: Regional Verification Commission (RVC): Responsible for verifying progress and determining whether countries, areas, and the region as a whole have eliminated endemic measles virus transmission. National Verification Committees (NVCs): Tasked with collecting, analyzing, and validating national data, preparing annual progress reports, and submitting documentation to the RVC. Post-Verification Needs: For countries that have achieved measles elimination, maintaining high levels of population immunity, ensuring verification-standard surveillance, and preparing for outbreak responses are critical to sustaining elimination. Conclusion: The guidelines emphasize the importance of independent verification processes, robust surveillance systems, and comprehensive documentation to confirm measles elimination. Countries unable to meet standard indicators may still achieve verification if sufficient alternative evidence is provided. Verification is an ongoing process, with annual assessments required until global measles eradication is achieved.
